glance.title: What this study found, at a glance
glance.note: In this model, heavier future rain puts more of Logroño's residents at flood risk, the planned green measures offset little of it, and greening all open space mainly protects the less vulnerable.

audiences.label: For citizens
audiences.level: General public — no science background needed
audiences.title: Will heavy rain flood more homes in Logroño, and do green spaces help?
audiences.lead: For every residential building in Logroño: how many residents are at risk when a short, heavy downpour floods the streets — today, with heavier future rain, and with more green space?

sections.p: REACHOUT computer flood maps for 15-minute downpours from storms expected every 2 years to once in 200 years. For each building: how deep the water gets nearby, how many people live there, and how socially vulnerable they are.

sections.h: Heavier rain puts more people at risk
sections.p: In every case examined: a few percent more residents at risk in the middle scenario, up to about one in ten more in the high one. How much depends on how much heavier the rain becomes, which is uncertain. Today's once-in-100-years flooding could come roughly twice as often, or more. Destination Earth data support the middle scenario's order of magnitude.

sections.h: The planned green measures help only a little
sections.p: As REACHOUT modelled them, they cut the number of residents at risk by a few percent at most, only for frequent storms, and not at all for the biggest ones. They do not offset heavier rain in this model.

sections.h: More green space helps — but not those who need it most
sections.p: Turning all open space green takes roughly one in ten to one in five of the residents at risk out of risk. But in every comparison, those who leave risk are less socially vulnerable than those who stay; the most vulnerable fifth benefits least.

sections.h: What it means, and what it cannot say
sections.p: Place green measures where vulnerable residents are at risk, not just where there is space, and re-check the planned measures with a model that includes sewers and storage. Uncertainties are large — one flood model without sewers, scenario rainfall, census-based vulnerability — so the direction of each finding is more reliable than its size.

audiences.closing: Heavier rain is expected, though by how much is uncertain; where green measures are placed decides who they protect.

audiences.label: For schools
audiences.title: Who is protected when a city goes green?
audiences.lead: Climate change makes heavy rain heavier. Cities can add green spaces, which let rain soak into the ground. This study asks a fair question: who does that protect?

sections.p: Logroño is a city in northern Spain. When a lot of rain falls in a short time, streets can flood: pluvial flooding, caused by rain, not by a river. Does heavier future rain put more people at risk? Do the planned green measures help? And when the city goes green, who is protected?

Scientists used flood maps from a computer model. For every home building they combined how deep the water gets nearby, how many people live there, and how vulnerable they are — for example young children or older people living alone. A '100-year storm' comes on average once in 100 years; storms from every 2 to every 200 years were tested.

Heavier future rain puts more people at risk in every case tested. The planned green measures help only a little, and not at all for the biggest storms. Turning all open space green helps more — roughly one in ten to one in five of the people at risk become safe — but mostly the less vulnerable. The most vulnerable fifth benefits least.

sections.h: The lesson: how science checks itself
sections.p: The method was first rebuilt independently with open tools, and every building got the same risk class. The flood maps matched places that really flooded, but that only partly confirmed the method. Every result comes from one model with large uncertainties (no sewers; nobody knows exactly how much heavier rain will get), so scientists trust the direction of a result more than its exact number.

audiences.closing: Being fair is part of the science: a good plan asks not only how much it helps, but whom.
